title: Bekker's De Betoverde Weereld: Enlightenment Argument That Satan Cannot Act in World
description: Balthasar Bekker, a Dutch Reformed minister, published De Betoverde Weereld (The World Bewitched) in 1691, a major Enlightenment challenge to the entire framework of witch prosecution. Unlike earlier skeptics who questioned procedure or questioned particular accused persons' guilt, Bekker argued from theological and natural philosophical principles that Satan — a spiritual being — was incapable of physical action in the material world and had been bound since the Incarnation. Therefore, he argued, all reported witch phenomena were natural or fraudulent, and all prosecution of witches for supernatural harm was based on a theological error. The book was sensational: Bekker was suspended from the ministry, but the work ran through multiple editions and translations.
historiographical_note: Stuart Clark's Thinking with Demons gives Bekker extensive treatment as the culminating expression of a particular strand of theological skepticism — one that worked from within Christianity to deny the operational premises of demonology rather than from secular rationalism. Clark shows that Bekker's argument was theologically serious and not obviously ridiculous to contemporaries, even though it was condemned. Andrew Fix's Fallen Angels: Bekker's World Bewitched (1999) provides full English-language analysis.
source_method: Bekker, De Betoverde Weereld (1691); Clark, Thinking with Demons (1997); Fix, Fallen Angels (1999)
